subject: Pharmacology
vignette: A 28-year-old woman with generalized tonic-clonic seizures has been well controlled on a single antiseizure medication for one year. She now presents with two days of severe epigastric pain radiating to her back, accompanied by nausea and repeated vomiting. Her serum lipase is 6 times the upper limit of normal, and a CT abdomen shows peripancreatic fat stranding without gallstones or a dilated common bile duct. She drinks alcohol only occasionally.
question: Which of her antiseizure medications is the most likely cause of her presentation?

options.text: Carbamazepine
Lamotrigine
Phenytoin
Valproate
Gabapentin

explanation_correct: Valproate is a classic cause of drug-induced pancreatitis. Other causative agents include diuretics (furosemide, HCTZ), glucocorticoids, alcohol, and azathioprine. Acute pancreatitis presents with epigastric pain radiating to the back, nausea and vomiting, and a markedly elevated lipase, as in this patient without gallstones or significant alcohol use.

explanation_incorrect.A: Carbamazepine causes hyponatremia via SIADH, agranulocytosis, aplastic anemia, and DRESS, but pancreatitis is not a classic association.
explanation_incorrect.B: Lamotrigine's major toxicity is a severe rash including Stevens-Johnson syndrome; it is not associated with pancreatitis.
explanation_incorrect.C: Phenytoin causes gingival hyperplasia, hirsutism, megaloblastic anemia, and DRESS, but not pancreatitis.
explanation_incorrect.E: Gabapentin is a relatively benign agent that can cause sedation and ataxia; pancreatitis is not among its classic adverse effects.

educationalObjective: Valproate, diuretics (furosemide, HCTZ), glucocorticoids, alcohol, and azathioprine are classic causes of drug-induced pancreatitis.

subject: Pharmacology
vignette: A 45-year-old man started taking erythromycin for community-acquired pneumonia one week ago. He now presents with jaundice, dark urine, and right upper quadrant discomfort. Laboratory studies show a conjugated hyperbilirubinemia of 6 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase of 340 U/L, and mildly elevated aminotransferases. Ultrasound of the biliary tree is normal.
question: Which of the following best describes the drug reaction responsible for his jaundice?

options.text: Acute cholestatic hepatitis from a macrolide
Fulminant hepatic necrosis from acetaminophen
Immune-mediated hemolysis of red blood cells
Obstruction of the common bile duct by gallstones
Granulomatous infiltration of the liver by sarcoidosis

explanation_correct: Macrolides such as erythromycin are the classic cause of acute cholestatic hepatitis with jaundice. The pattern is cholestatic — a disproportionately elevated alkaline phosphatase with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia and only mild aminotransferase elevation — which appears within days to weeks of starting the drug, as seen here.

explanation_incorrect.B: Acetaminophen causes massive hepatic necrosis with strikingly high aminotransferases and fulminant liver failure, and the patient took erythromycin, not acetaminophen.
explanation_incorrect.C: Hemolysis causes an unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia without dark urine from conjugated bilirubin, and would be associated with anemia rather than a cholestatic enzyme pattern.
explanation_incorrect.D: Gallstone obstruction is excluded here by the normal biliary ultrasound, and the temporal relationship to erythromycin points to a drug reaction.
explanation_incorrect.E: Sarcoidosis can cause granulomatous hepatitis but is a chronic, systemic process not triggered by a drug course one week ago.

educationalObjective: Macrolides (eg, erythromycin) cause acute cholestatic hepatitis and jaundice.

subject: Pharmacology
vignette: A 64-year-old woman recently started therapy for osteoporosis. She takes one tablet with only a small sip of water immediately before lying down for bed. Three weeks later she presents with retrosternal pain that is worse when swallowing solids. Physical examination is unremarkable, and oral candidiasis is absent.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate counseling to prevent recurrence of her symptoms?

options.text: Take the medication with a full glass of water while remaining upright for at least 30 minutes
Crush the tablet and mix it with applesauce before lying down
Take the medication at bedtime with an antacid to buffer its effects
Switch immediately to intravenous glucocorticoid therapy for osteoporosis
Add a proton pump inhibitor and continue taking the tablet with a sip of water at bedtime

explanation_correct: This is medication-induced esophagitis from a bisphosphonate, one of the classic offenders along with potassium chloride, NSAIDs, ferrous sulfate, and tetracyclines. Pills injure the esophagus where it is anatomically narrowed (eg, near the level of the aortic arch), and the caustic effect is minimized by taking the medication upright with a full glass of water and remaining upright afterward.

explanation_incorrect.B: Crushing the tablet does not prevent the local caustic effect — bisphosphonates must not be crushed, and lying down immediately after dosing is the problem, not the pill form itself.
explanation_incorrect.C: An antacid does not prevent the mechanical and chemical contact injury, and taking the dose at bedtime while lying down recreates the exact circumstances that caused the esophagitis.
explanation_incorrect.D: Systemic glucocorticoids are not an osteoporosis treatment here — in fact, glucocorticoids themselves cause adverse effects — and her reaction is local and preventable by proper dosing technique.
explanation_incorrect.E: Continuing the same dosing technique (small sip, bedtime, lying down) would reproduce the injury; acid suppression does not address the direct caustic contact with the esophageal mucosa.

educationalObjective: Medication-induced esophagitis (KCl, NSAIDs, bisphosphonates, ferrous sulfate, tetracyclines) is prevented by taking pills upright with ample water.

subject: Pharmacology
vignette: A 22-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 30 hours after ingesting a large quantity of extra-strength analgesic tablets in a suicide attempt. She is now confused and icteric, with vomiting. Laboratory studies show AST 8,200 U/L, ALT 9,100 U/L, INR 3.4, and a pH of 7.28. Her prothrombin time is markedly prolonged.
question: What is the mechanism of her acute liver injury?

options.text: T cell–mediated hypersensitivity causing granulomatous inflammation
Cytochrome P450–generated toxic metabolite that depletes glutathione stores
Direct cholestatic injury to the bile canaliculi
Microvesicular steatosis from impaired mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation
Budd-Chiari syndrome from hepatic vein thrombosis

explanation_correct: Acetaminophen overdose causes focal to massive hepatic necrosis: its toxic metabolite NAPQI is generated by cytochrome P450 enzymes and depletes glutathione stores, causing direct hepatocyte death. The treatment is N-acetylcysteine, which replenishes glutathione. Valproate and ingestion of the Amanita phalloides (death cap) mushroom cause the same pattern of focal to massive hepatic necrosis.

explanation_incorrect.A: T cell–mediated hypersensitivity describes DRESS and idiosyncratic drug reactions such as hepatitis from rifampin or isoniazid, not the predictable dose-related necrosis of acetaminophen overdose.
explanation_incorrect.C: Cholestatic injury elevates alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin out of proportion to aminotransferases; this patient has extreme aminotransferase levels consistent with massive hepatocyte necrosis.
explanation_incorrect.D: Impaired mitochondrial beta-oxidation with microvesicular steatosis is the mechanism of valproate-related hyperammonemic toxicity, but acetaminophen injures through NAPQI-mediated glutathione depletion and direct necrosis.
explanation_incorrect.E: Budd-Chiari syndrome is a vascular outflow obstruction presenting with hepatomegaly and ascites, unrelated to drug ingestion.

educationalObjective: Acetaminophen causes hepatic necrosis via CYP450-generated NAPQI that depletes glutathione; N-acetylcysteine is the antidote.

subject: Pharmacology
vignette: A 56-year-old man with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes was started on an oral antidiabetic agent two weeks ago. He now reports several loose, nonbloody bowel movements daily without fever or tenesmus. Stool studies are negative for leukocytes and pathogens, and his symptoms have been present since the medication was begun.
question: Which of his medications is the most likely cause of his diarrhea?

options.text: Clostridioides difficile colitis from recent clindamycin use
Irritant laxative overuse
Metformin
Ondansetron
Celiac disease unmasked by drug therapy

explanation_correct: Metformin is one of the classic antidiabetic agents causing drug-induced diarrhea, along with acarbose and pramlintide. The temporal relationship between starting the drug and the onset of loose, noninflammatory stools (negative stool studies, no fever) identifies a direct medication side effect rather than an infectious or inflammatory process.

explanation_incorrect.A: C difficile colitis follows antibiotic exposure such as clindamycin and produces fever, leukocytosis, and inflammatory stool findings — none of which are present here.
explanation_incorrect.B: Laxative overuse is a behavioral cause of diarrhea not supported by the history, and the tight temporal link to starting diabetes therapy points to the drug itself.
explanation_incorrect.D: Ondansetron is a 5-HT3 antagonist whose GI adverse effect is constipation, the opposite of this patient's problem.
explanation_incorrect.E: Celiac disease is a chronic gluten-driven enteropathy; there is nothing in this acute, medication-linked presentation to suggest it.

educationalObjective: Acarbose, metformin, and pramlintide are antidiabetic agents classically causing diarrhea.
